name: Safale American
notes: Clean, neutral American ale strain.

name: Safale English
notes: Fast, flocculent English ale.

name: Safale K-97
notes: German ale / Kölsch style.

name: Safale BE-256
notes: Belgian abbey ales.

name: Safbrew T-58
notes: Spicy, peppery Belgian character.

name: Safale WB-06
notes: Banana & clove for wheat beers.

name: Saflager W-34/70
notes: Classic Weihenstephan lager strain.

name: Nottingham
notes: Neutral, very versatile English ale.

name: Windsor
notes: Fruity, full-bodied English ale.

name: London ESB
notes: Low attenuation English bitter strain.

name: BRY-97 West Coast
notes: Clean American ale.

name: Verdant IPA
notes: Apricot notes; great for hazy IPA.

name: Voss Kveik
notes: Orange-peel esters, ferments very warm.

name: Belle Saison
notes: Dry, spicy saison.

name: Munich Classic
notes: Bavarian wheat.

name: Novalager
notes: Clean lager at ale temperatures.

name: American Ale
notes: Chico strain; clean and crisp.

name: Irish Ale
notes: Great for stouts.

name: London Ale III
notes: Soft, fruity; NEIPA favourite.

name: London ESB Ale
notes: Fuller's strain.

name: Weihenstephan Weizen
notes: Classic banana and clove.

name: French Saison
notes: Very attenuative.

name: Belgian Saison
notes: Dupont strain; may stall — keep warm.

name: Juice
notes: Hazy IPA favourite.

name: Lactobacillus Blend
notes: For kettle sours.

name: EC-1118 Champagne
notes: For bottle conditioning or very dry beers.

name: SafLager German Lager
notes: Popular lager yeast strain. Produces wide range of continental lagers and pilsners. Clean finish. Best for: Wide range of lagers and pilsners. Attenuation not in source data; 73–78% is typical for this type. Check the lab's spec.

name: SafBrew Ale
notes: General purpose ale yeast, widely used. Very consistent, clean finish. High attenuation and good flavor profile. Best for: Most ales. Attenuation not in source data; 72–78% is typical for this type. Check the lab's spec.

name: Lalvin
notes: Rapid starter with constant and complete fermentation. Ability to metabolize high amounts (20-40%) of malic acid. Partial metabolism of malic acid helps soften the wine. May produce significant esters, making it a good choice for concentrates. Best for: Young wines such as nouveau, blush and sugar white. Attenuation not in source data; 90–98% is typical for this type. Check the lab's spec.

name: Lalvin
notes: Recommended for white variety wines such as Chardonnay and Rose as well as Mead. Low foaming, quick fermenting, forming a compact lees at the end of fermentation. Use yeast nutrients if making mead. Saccharomyces Cerevisiae. Best for: White wines such as Chardonnay and Rose. Also good for mead. Attenuation not in source data; 90–98% is typical for this type. Check the lab's spec.

name: Lalvin
notes: Used for white grape varieties. Rapid starter with constant and complete fermentation. Capable of surviving difficult conditions such as low nutrient or high SO2 levels. Has low volatile action. Best for: Souvingnon Blanc, Chenin Blanc and Seyval. Attenuation not in source data; 90–98% is typical for this type. Check the lab's spec.

name: Lalvin
notes: RC212 recommended for red variety wines and high gravity beers. Alcohol tolerance in the 12-14% range. Low foaming and moderate speed fermenting. Saccharomyces Cerevisiae. Best for: Red wines. Attenuation not in source data; 90–98% is typical for this type. Check the lab's spec.

name: German Ale II
notes: Strong sulfer component will reduce with aging. Clean flavor, but with more ester production than regular German Ale Yeast. Best for: Kolsch, Alt and German Pale Ales. Attenuation not in source data; 72–78% is typical for this type. Check the lab's spec.

name: British Ale
notes: This yeast has higher attenuation than the White Labs English Ale yeast strains. Produces a malty flavored beer. Best for: Excellent for all English style ales including bitters, pale ale, porters and brown ale. Attenuation not in source data; 72–78% is typical for this type. Check the lab's spec.

name: Bedford British Ale
notes: High attenuation. Ferments dry with high flocculation. Distinctive ester profile. Good for most English ale styles. Best for: English style ales - bitter, pale, porter and brown ale. Attenuation not in source data; 72–78% is typical for this type. Check the lab's spec.

name: Dry English Ale
notes: Clean, Highly flocculant, and highly attentive yeast. Similar to White labs English Ale yeast, but more attentive. Suitable for high gravity ales. Best for: Pale Ales, Amber, ESB, Brown Ales, Strong Ales. Attenuation not in source data; 72–78% is typical for this type. Check the lab's spec.

name: East Coast Ale
notes: White labs "Brewer Patriot" strain can be used to reproduce many of the American versions of classic beer styles. Very clean with low esters. Best for: American Ales, Golden ales, Blonde Ale, Pale Ale and German Alt styles. Attenuation not in source data; 72–78% is typical for this type. Check the lab's spec.

name: Australian Ale Yeast
notes: White Labs entry for Australian Ales. Produces a clean, malty finish with pleasant ester character. Bready character. Can ferment clean at high temperatures. Best for: Australian Ales, English Ales. Attenuation not in source data; 72–78% is typical for this type. Check the lab's spec.

name: European Ale
notes: Malty, Northern European ale yeast. Low ester production, low sulfer, gives a clean profile. Low attenuation contributes to malty taste. Best for: Alt, Kolsch, malty English Ales, Fruit beers. Attenuation not in source data; 72–78% is typical for this type. Check the lab's spec.

name: London Ale
notes: Dry, malty ale yeast. Produces a complex, oak flavored ester character. Hop bitterness comes through well. Best for: Classic British Pale Ales, Bitters and Stouts. Attenuation not in source data; 72–78% is typical for this type. Check the lab's spec.

name: Essex Ale Yeast
notes: Flavorful British yeast with a drier finish than many ale yeasts. Bready and fruity in character. Well suited for top cropping (collecting). Does not flocculate as much as WLP005 or WLP002. Best for: British milds, pale ales, bitters, stouts. Attenuation not in source data; 72–78% is typical for this type. Check the lab's spec.

name: Burton Ale
notes: Burton-on-trent yeast produces a complex character. Flavors include apple, pear, and clover honey. Best for: All English styles including Pale Ale, IPA, Porter, Stout and Bitters. Attenuation not in source data; 72–78% is typical for this type. Check the lab's spec.

name: Southwold Ale
notes: From Suffolk county. Products complex fruity and citrus flavors. Slight sulfer production, but this will fade with aging. Best for: British bitters and pale ales. Attenuation not in source data; 72–78% is typical for this type. Check the lab's spec.

name: Premium Bitter Ale
notes: From Staffordshire England. Mild, but complex estery flavor. High attenuation - ferments strong and dry. Suitable for high gravity beers. Best for: All English ales including bitters, milds, ESB, Porter, Stout and Barley Wine. Attenuation not in source data; 72–78% is typical for this type. Check the lab's spec.

name: Edinburgh Ale
notes: Malty strong ale yeast. Reproduces complex, malty, flavorful schottish ales. Hop character comes through well. Best for: Strong Scottish style ales, ESB, Irish Reds. Attenuation not in source data; 72–78% is typical for this type. Check the lab's spec.

name: Klassic Ale Yeast
notes: Traditional English Ale style yeast. Produces ester character, and allows hop flavor through. Leaves a slightly sweet malt character in ales. Best for: Bitters, milds, porters stouts and scottish ale styles. Attenuation not in source data; 72–78% is typical for this type. Check the lab's spec.

name: Dusseldorf Alt Yeast
notes: Traditional alternative yeast from Dusseldorf, Germany. Produces clean, slightly sweet alt beers. Does not accentuate hop flavor like WLP029 does. Best for: Alt biers, Dusseldorf Alts, German Ales. Attenuation not in source data; 72–78% is typical for this type. Check the lab's spec.

name: Yorkshire Square Ale Yeast
notes: This yeast produces a malty but well balanced profile. Expect toasty flavors with malt driven esters. Highly flocculent and a good choice for many English ales. Best for: English pale ales, English brown ales and Mild ales. Attenuation not in source data; 72–78% is typical for this type. Check the lab's spec.

name: Manchester Ale Yeast
notes: Top fermenting strain that is good for top-cropping. Moderately flocculent with a clean, dry finish. Low ester profile for producing a balanced English ale. Best for: English style ales. Attenuation not in source data; 72–78% is typical for this type. Check the lab's spec.

name: Nottingham Ale Yeast
notes: British style of ale yeast with a very dry finish and high attenuation. Medium to low fruit and fusel alcohol production. Good top fermenting yeast for cropping. Best for: British ales, pale ales, ambers, porters and stouts. Attenuation not in source data; 72–78% is typical for this type. Check the lab's spec.

name: Pacific Ale
notes: Popular yeast from the Pacific Northwest. Leaves a clear and malty profile. More fruity than WLP002. Suitable for many English and American styles. Best for: English & American ales including milds, bitters, IPA, porters and English stouts. Attenuation not in source data; 72–78% is typical for this type. Check the lab's spec.

name: California Ale V
notes: Similar to White Labs California Ale Yeast, but slightly lower attenuation leaves a fuller bodied beer. Best for: American style Pales, Ambers, Browns, IPAs, American Strong Ale. Attenuation not in source data; 72–78% is typical for this type. Check the lab's spec.

name: American Ale Yeast Blend
notes: A blend that celebrates WLP001 (California Ale Yeast's) clean, neutral fermentation. This strain is versatile and adds two other yeast strains that are also clean/neutral in flavor to add a bit of complexity - almost a lager like finish. Best for: American ales with clean finish. Attenuation not in source data; 72–78% is typical for this type. Check the lab's spec.

name: Cream Ale Yeast Blend
notes: A blend of ale and lager yeast strains that work together to create a clean, light American lager style ale. A pleasing estery aroma may be perceived. Hop flavors and bitterness are slightly subdued. Best for: Cream Ale, Hybrids. Attenuation not in source data; 72–78% is typical for this type. Check the lab's spec.

name: San Diego Super Yeast
notes: A super clean, super-fast fermenting strain. A low ester-producing strain that results in a balanced, neutral flavor and aroma profile. Alcohol-tolerant and very versatile for a wide variety of styles. Similar to California Ale Yeast WLP001 but it generally ferments faster. Best for: IPAs, American ales. Attenuation not in source data; 72–78% is typical for this type. Check the lab's spec.

name: Super High Gravity Ale
notes: Ferments up to 25% alcohol content. Flavor may vary greatly depending on beer alcohol. English like esters at low gravity, but will become more wine-like as alcohol exceeds 16% ABV. Refer to White Labs web page for tips on fermenting high gravity ales. Best for: Very high gravity beers and barley wine up to 25% alcohol. Attenuation not in source data; 72–78% is typical for this type. Check the lab's spec.

name: American Hefeweizen Ale
notes: Produces a much smaller amount of clove and banana flavor than the German Hefeweizen White Labs yeast. Some sulfur, and creates desired cloudy look. Best for: Oregon style American Hefeweizen. Attenuation not in source data; 72–77% is typical for this type. Check the lab's spec.

name: Bavarian Weizen Yeast
notes: Former yeast lab W51 strain. Produces a classic German style wheat beer with moderately high, spicy, phenolic overtones reminiscent of cloves. Best for: Bavarian Weizen and wheat beers. Attenuation not in source data; 72–77% is typical for this type. Check the lab's spec.

name: Hefeweizen IV Ale
notes: Large clove and phenolic aroma, but with minimal banana flavor. Citrus and apricot notes. Crisp and drinkable, with some sulfur production. Best for: German style Hefeweizen. Attenuation not in source data; 72–77% is typical for this type. Check the lab's spec.

name: Belgian Wit Ale
notes: Phenolic and tart. The original yeast used to produce Wit in Belgium. Best for: Belgian Wit. Attenuation not in source data; 75–83% is typical for this type. Check the lab's spec.

name: Belgian Wit II
notes: Less phenolic than WLP400 (Belgian Wit Ale) but more spicy. Leaves a little more sweetness and flocculation is higher than WLP400. Best for: Belgian Wit, Spiced Ale, Wheat Ales and Specialty Beers. Attenuation not in source data; 75–83% is typical for this type. Check the lab's spec.

name: Trappist Ale
notes: Distinctive fruitiness and plum characteristics. Excellent for high gravity beers. Best for: Trappist Ale, Dubbel, Trippel, Belgian Ales. Attenuation not in source data; 75–83% is typical for this type. Check the lab's spec.

name: Bastogne Belgian Ale
notes: High gravity Trappist ale yeast. Creates a dry beer with a slightly acidic finish. Cleaner finish and slightly less spicy than WLP500 or WLP530. Best for: High gravity beers, Belgian ales, Dubbels, Trippels. Attenuation not in source data; 75–83% is typical for this type. Check the lab's spec.

name: Antwerp Ale Yeast
notes: Clean, almost lager like Belgian ale yeast. Good for Belgian pale and amber ales or with other Belgian yeasts in a blend. Biscuity, ale like aroma present. Hop flavors are accentuated. Slight sulfur during fermentation, and a lager like flavor profile. Best for: Belgian pale and amber ales. Attenuation not in source data; 75–83% is typical for this type. Check the lab's spec.

name: Abbey IV Ale Yeast
notes: An authentic Trappist style ale yeast. Use for Belgian ales including abbey ales (dubbels, tripels). Fruit character is medium - between WLP500 (high) and WLP530 (low). Best for: Trappist Belgian Ales, Dubbels, Tripels and Specialty ales. Attenuation not in source data; 75–83% is typical for this type. Check the lab's spec.

name: Belgian Strong Ale Yeast
notes: From the Ardennes region of Belgium, this classic strain produces moderate esters and spicy phenolic character. Results in a dry but balanced finish. Use for dark or strong abbey ales. Best for: Belgian dark strongs, Abbey ales and Christmas beers. Attenuation not in source data; 75–83% is typical for this type. Check the lab's spec.

name: Belgian Ale
notes: Phenolic and spicy flavors. Complex profile, with less fruitiness than White's Trappist Ale strain. Best for: Belgian Ales, Saisons, Belgian Reds, Belgian Browns, White beers. Attenuation not in source data; 75–83% is typical for this type. Check the lab's spec.

name: Belgian Saison II Yeast
notes: Saison strain with a more fruity ester profile than WLP565 (Belgian Saison I Yeast). Moderately phenolic with a clove-like characteristic in finished beer flavor and aroma. Ferments quickly. Best for: Belgian or French Saison. Attenuation not in source data; 75–83% is typical for this type. Check the lab's spec.

name: Belgian Style Saison Ale Yeast Blend
notes: This blend melds Belgian style ale and Saison strains. The strains work in harmony to create complex, fruity aromas and flavors. The blend of yeast strains encourages complete fermentation in a timely manner. Phenolic, spicy, earthy, and clove like flavor. Best for: Belgian and French Saison. Attenuation not in source data; 75–83% is typical for this type. Check the lab's spec.

name: Belgian Golden Ale
notes: Combination of fruitiness and phenolic characters dominate the profile. Some sulfur which will dissipate following fermentation. Best for: Belgian Ales, Dubbel, Grand Cru, Belgian Holiday Ale. Attenuation not in source data; 75–83% is typical for this type. Check the lab's spec.

name: Belgian Style Ale Yeast Blend
notes: Blend of two trappist ale yeasts and one Belgian ale yeast. Creates a versatile blend to be used for Trappist and other Belgian style ales. Best for: Trappist and other Belgian ales. Attenuation not in source data; 75–83% is typical for this type. Check the lab's spec.

name: Berliner Weisse Blend
notes: A blend of a traditional German Weizen yeast and Lactobacillus to create a subtle, tart, drinkable beer. Can take several months to develop tart character. Perfect for traditional Berliner Weisse. Best for: Berliner Weisse. Attenuation not in source data; 80–90% is typical for this type. Check the lab's spec.

name: Brettanomyces Claussenii
notes: Low intensity Brett character. Originally isolated from strong English stock beer, in the early 20th century. The Brett flavors produced are more subtle than WLP650 and WLP653. More aroma than flavor contribution. Fruity, pineapple like aroma. Best for: Sour ales (in secondary). Attenuation not in source data; 80–90% is typical for this type. Check the lab's spec.

name: Brettanomyces Bruxellensis
notes: Medium intensity Brett character. Classic strain used in secondary fermentation for Belgian style beers and lambics. One Trappist brewery uses this strain in secondary fermentation. Best for: Belgian sour ales and lambics (in secondary). Attenuation not in source data; 80–90% is typical for this type. Check the lab's spec.

name: Brettanomyces Lambicus
notes: Use in secondary. High intensity Brett character. Defines the "Brett character": Horsey, smoky and spicy flavors. As the name suggests, this strain is found most often in Lambic style beers, which are spontaneously fermented beers. Best for: Lambics and Flanders/Sour Brown ales. Attenuation not in source data; 80–90% is typical for this type. Check the lab's spec.

name: Belgian Sour Mix 1
notes: Note: Bacteria to use in secondary only. A unique blend perfect for Belgian style beers. Includes Brettanomyces, Saccharomyces, and the bacterial strains Lactobacillus and Pediococcus. Best for: Belgian sour beers (in secondary). Attenuation not in source data; 80–90% is typical for this type. Check the lab's spec.

name: American Farmhouse Blend
notes: Inspired by local American brewers crafting semi- traditional Belgian-style ales. This blend creates a complex flavor profile with a moderate level of sourness. It consists of a traditional farmhouse yeast strain and Brettanomyces. Great yeast for farmhouse styles. Best for: Saisons, Farmhouse Ales. Attenuation not in source data; 80–90% is typical for this type. Check the lab's spec.

name: Malolactic Bacteria
notes: Bacteria for use in secondary. Malolactic fermentation is the conversion of malic acid to lactic acid by bacteria from the lactic acid bacteria family. Lactic acid is less acidic than malic acid, which in turn decreases acidity and helps to soften. Best for: Primarily wine. Attenuation not in source data; 72–78% is typical for this type. Check the lab's spec.

name: Lactobacillus Bacteria
notes: Bacteria for use in secondary. This lactic acid bacteria produces moderate levels of acidity and sour flavors found in lambics, Berliner Weiss, sour brown ale and gueze. Best for: Lambic, Berliner Weiss, Sour Brown and Gueze (secondary). Attenuation not in source data; 80–90% is typical for this type. Check the lab's spec.

name: Flor Sherry Yeast
notes: This yeast develops a film (flor) on the surface of the wine. Creates green almond, granny smith and nougat characteristics found in sherry. Can also be used for Port, Madeira and other sweet styles. For use in secondary fermentation. Slow fermentor. Best for: Sherry wine yeast. Attenuation not in source data; 90–98% is typical for this type. Check the lab's spec.

name: Sake Yeast
notes: For use in rice based fermentations. For sake, use this yeast in conjunction with Koji (to produce fermentable sugar). WLP705 produces full body sake character, and subtle fragrance. Alcohol tolerance to 16%. Best for: Sake wine yeast. Attenuation not in source data; 90–98% is typical for this type. Check the lab's spec.

name: Champagne Yeast
notes: Can tolerate alcohol up to 17%. For Barley Wine or Meads. Best for: Wine, Mead and Cider. Attenuation not in source data; 90–98% is typical for this type. Check the lab's spec.

name: Avize Wine Yeast
notes: Champagne isolate used for complexity in whites. Contributes elegance, especially in barrel fermented Chardonnays. Alcohol tolerance to 15%. Best for: Chardonnay. Attenuation not in source data; 90–98% is typical for this type. Check the lab's spec.

name: Sweet Mead/Wine
notes: Lower attenuation than White Labs Champagne Yeast. Leaves some residual sweetness as well as fruity flavor. Alcohol concentration up to 15%. Best for: Sweet Mead, Wine and Cider. Attenuation not in source data; 90–98% is typical for this type. Check the lab's spec.

name: Steinberg-Geisenheim Wine
notes: German origin wine yeast. High fruit/ester production. Moderate fermentation characteristics and cold tolerant. Best for: Riesling wines. Attenuation not in source data; 90–98% is typical for this type. Check the lab's spec.

name: Chardonnay White Wine Yeast
notes: Dry wine yeast. Slight ester production, low sulfur dioxide production. Enhances varietal character. WLP730 is a good choice for all white and blush wines, including Chablis, Chenin Blanc, Semillon, and Sauvignon Blanc. Fermentation speed is moderate. Best for: Chardonnay Wine. Attenuation not in source data; 90–98% is typical for this type. Check the lab's spec.

name: French White Wine Yeast
notes: Classic yeast for white wine fermentation. Slow to moderate fermenter and foam producer. Gives an enhanced creamy texture. Alcohol Tolerance: 16%. Best for: French white wines. Attenuation not in source data; 90–98% is typical for this type. Check the lab's spec.

name: Merlot Red Wine Yeast
notes: Neutral, low fusel alcohol production. Will ferment to dryness, alcohol tolerance to 18%. Vigorous fermenter. WLP740 is well suited for Merlot, Shiraz, Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Cabernet, Sauvignon Blanc, and Semillon. Alcohol Tolerance: 18%. Best for: Merlot, Shiraz, Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Cabernet, Sauvignon Blanc, and Semillon. Attenuation not in source data; 90–98% is typical for this type. Check the lab's spec.

name: Assmanshausen Wine Yeast
notes: German red wine yeast, which results in spicy, fruit aromas. Perfect for Pinot Noir and Zinfandel. Slow to moderate fermenter which is cold tolerant. Alcohol Tolerance: 16%. Best for: Pinot Noir and Zinfandel. Attenuation not in source data; 90–98% is typical for this type. Check the lab's spec.

name: French Red Wine Yeast
notes: Classic Bordeaux yeast for red wine fermentations. Moderate fermentation characteristics. Tolerates lower fermentation temperatures. Rich, smooth flavor profile. Alcohol Tolerance: 17%. Best for: Bordeaux. Attenuation not in source data; 90–98% is typical for this type. Check the lab's spec.

name: Cabernet Red Wine Yeast
notes: High temperature tolerance. Moderate fermentation speed. Excellent for full-bodied red wines, ester production complements flavor. WLP760 is also suitable for Merlot, Chardonnay, Chianti, Chenin Blanc, and Sauvignon Blanc. Alcohol Tolerance: 16%. Best for: Merlot, Chardonnay, Chianti, Chenin Blanc, and Sauvignon Blanc. Attenuation not in source data; 90–98% is typical for this type. Check the lab's spec.

name: Suremain Burgundy Wine Yeast
notes: Emphasizes fruit aromas in barrel fermentations. High nutrient requirement to avoid volatile acidity production. Alcohol Tolerance: 16%. Best for: Burgundy. Attenuation not in source data; 90–98% is typical for this type. Check the lab's spec.

name: English Cider Yeast
notes: Classic Cider yeast. Ferments dry, but retains apple flavor. Some sulfer produced during fermentation will fade with age. Best for: Cider, Wine and High Gravity Beer. Attenuation not in source data; 90–98% is typical for this type. Check the lab's spec.

name: Pilsner Lager
notes: Classic pilsner strain from Czech Republic. Dry with a malty finish. Best for: European Pilsners, Bohemian Pilsner. Attenuation not in source data; 73–78% is typical for this type. Check the lab's spec.

name: Czech Budejovice Lager
notes: Dry and crisp with low diacetyl production. From Southern Czech Republic. Best for: Bohemian Style Pilsner. Attenuation not in source data; 73–78% is typical for this type. Check the lab's spec.

name: San Francisco Lager
notes: Produces "California Common" style beer. Best for: California and Premium Lagers, all American Lagers. Attenuation not in source data; 73–78% is typical for this type. Check the lab's spec.

name: Belgian Lager Yeast
notes: Clean, crisp European lager yeast with low sulfur production. The strain originates from a very old brewery in West Belgium. Great for European style pilsners, dark lagers, Vienna lager, and American style lagers. Best for: European style pilsners, dark lagers, Vienna lager, and American style lagers. Attenuation not in source data; 75–83% is typical for this type. Check the lab's spec.

name: Octoberfest/Marzen Lager
notes: Produces a malty, bock style beer. Does not finish as dry or as fast as White's German Lager yeast. Longer lagering or starter recommended. Best for: Marzen, Oktoberfest, European Lagers, Bocks, Munich Helles. Attenuation not in source data; 73–78% is typical for this type. Check the lab's spec.

name: German Bock Lager
notes: Produces beer that has balanced malt and hop character. From Southern Bavaria. Best for: Bocks, Doppelbocks, Oktoberfest, Vienna, Helles, some American Pilsners. Attenuation not in source data; 73–78% is typical for this type. Check the lab's spec.

name: Southern German Lager
notes: Malty finish and balanced aroma. Strong fermenter, slight sulfur and low diacetyl. Best for: German Pilsner, Helles, Oktoberfest, Marzen, Bocks. Attenuation not in source data; 73–78% is typical for this type. Check the lab's spec.

name: American Lager Yeast
notes: Dry and clean with very slight apple fruitiness. Minimal sulfer and diacetyl. Best for: All American Style Lagers -- both light and dark. Attenuation not in source data; 73–78% is typical for this type. Check the lab's spec.

name: Munich Helles
notes: Possible Augustiner Strain. This yeast helps to produce a malty, but balanced traditional Munich-style lager. Clean and strong fermenter, it's great for a variety of lager styles ranging from Helles to Rauchbier. Best for: Munich Helles, Oktoberfest. Attenuation not in source data; 72–78% is typical for this type. Check the lab's spec.

name: Cry Havoc
notes: Licensed by White Labs from Charlie Papazian, author of "The Complete Joy of Home Brewing". This yeast was used to brew many of his original recipes. Diverse strain can ferment at ale and lager temps. Best for: All American Style Lagers -- both light and dark. Attenuation not in source data; 73–78% is typical for this type. Check the lab's spec.

name: Zurich Lager
notes: Swiss style lager yeast. Sulfer and diacetyl production is minimal. May be used for high gravity lagers with proper care. Best for: Swiss style lager, and high gravity lagers (over 11% ABV). Attenuation not in source data; 73–78% is typical for this type. Check the lab's spec.

name: Old Bavarian Lager
notes: Southern Germany/Bavarian lager yeast. Finishes malty with a slight ester profile. Best for: Oktoberfest, Marzen, Bock and Dark Lagers. Attenuation not in source data; 73–78% is typical for this type. Check the lab's spec.

name: Mexican Lager
notes: From Mexico City - produces a clean lager beer with a crisp finish. Good for mexican style beers. Best for: Mexican style light and dark lagers. Attenuation not in source data; 73–78% is typical for this type. Check the lab's spec.

name: American Wheat Ale
notes: Dry, Crisp, tart beer in the American Hefeweizen style. Low flocculation aids in producing desired chill haze. Best for: American Wheat, Berlin Weiss, Hefeweizen. Attenuation not in source data; 72–78% is typical for this type. Check the lab's spec.

name: British Cask Ale
notes: A great choice for any cask conditioned British Ale. Produces nice malt profile with a hint of fruit. Finishes dry and slightly tart. Best for: British Ales. Attenuation not in source data; 72–78% is typical for this type. Check the lab's spec.

name: London Ale Yeast
notes: Dry finish, bold, rich flavor, some fruit profile and a crisp finish. Best for: English Ales, Bitters, IPAs, Brown Ale. Attenuation not in source data; 72–78% is typical for this type. Check the lab's spec.

name: Wyeast Ale Blend
notes: Blend of ale strains designed to provide quick starts, good flavor, balance and flocculation. Balanced finish suitable for most American and British ale styles. Best for: American and British Ale Styles. Attenuation not in source data; 72–78% is typical for this type. Check the lab's spec.

name: British Ale Yeast
notes: Fruity, tart, dry crisp finish. Very well balanced. Best for: All British Ales, Pales, Bitters, English Strong Ale. Attenuation not in source data; 72–78% is typical for this type. Check the lab's spec.

name: Whitbread Ale
notes: Slightly more fruity and malty than Wyeast's British Ale. Clear and highly flocculant. Best for: Whitbread Ale, British Ales, Pales, Bitters. Attenuation not in source data; 72–78% is typical for this type. Check the lab's spec.

name: Ringwood Ale
notes: European ale yeast. Highly flocculant with complex, clear, but malty profile. Slightly fruity ester. Best for: Ringwood Ale, Brown Ales. Attenuation not in source data; 72–78% is typical for this type. Check the lab's spec.

name: American Ale II
notes: Clean, tart, nutty flavor. More fruity than Wyeast American Ale yeast. Best for: All American Ales, Brown Ales, Barley Wine. Attenuation not in source data; 72–78% is typical for this type. Check the lab's spec.

name: Thames Valley Ale
notes: Clean, complex flavor. Low in fruit, low in esters, rich in flavor. Hops come through well. Best for: British Bitters, ESB, India Pale Ale, English Strong Ale. Attenuation not in source data; 72–78% is typical for this type. Check the lab's spec.

name: Northwest Ale
